description: Hemoglobin is an iron-rich protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body.
low_implication: Low levels indicate anemia, which can cause fatigue, weakness, pale skin, or shortness of breath. Common causes include iron deficiency, vitamin deficiencies, blood loss, or bone marrow disorders.
high_implication: High levels (polycythemia) may result from chronic dehydration, smoking, chronic lung disease (COPD), high altitude living, or bone marrow overproduction.
lifestyle_guidance: Include iron-rich foods (spinach, lentils, red meat, fortified cereals) and vitamin C to enhance iron absorption. Stay well-hydrated.
clinical_follow_up: Check Serum Ferritin, Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC), and Vitamin B12/Folate levels if low.
source: WHO Guidelines on Anemia & NIH MedlinePlus

description: Red Blood Cells (erythrocytes) carry oxygen throughout the body and remove carbon dioxide.
low_implication: Decreased count suggests anemia, chronic illness, nutritional deficiencies (iron, B12), or hemolysis.
high_implication: Elevated count (erythrocytosis) can occur with dehydration, sleep apnea, smoking, or polycythemia vera.
lifestyle_guidance: Maintain a balanced nutrient-dense diet and ensure adequate fluid intake.
clinical_follow_up: Complete hemogram with peripheral blood smear examination.

description: White Blood Cells (leukocytes) are the immune system's primary defense against infections, inflammation, and diseases.
low_implication: Leukopenia increases susceptibility to infections; causes include viral infections, autoimmune conditions, bone marrow suppression, or medication side effects.
high_implication: Leukocytosis often signifies bacterial or viral infection, acute physical stress, systemic inflammation, allergies, or tissue damage.
lifestyle_guidance: Practice good hygiene, maintain a diet rich in antioxidants and vitamins, and avoid exposure to contagious illnesses.
clinical_follow_up: Differential Leukocyte Count (DLC), CRP, or repeat CBC if symptoms persist.
source: NIH MedlinePlus White Blood Cell Reference

description: Platelets (thrombocytes) are specialized cell fragments essential for blood clotting and wound healing.
low_implication: Thrombocytopenia can heighten the risk of bruising, petechiae, or prolonged bleeding; triggers include viral infections (e.g. dengue), immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), or medication reactions.
high_implication: Thrombocytosis can be reactive (due to acute inflammation, infection, iron deficiency) or essential, potentially increasing blood clot risk.
lifestyle_guidance: Avoid high-impact contact activities if platelets are low. Avoid self-medicating with aspirin or NSAIDs without physician advice.
clinical_follow_up: Repeat platelet count with peripheral smear examination; rule out clumping artifact.

description: Mean Corpuscular Volume measures the average size of your red blood cells.
low_implication: Microcytosis (low MCV) is classic for iron deficiency anemia or thalassemia trait.
high_implication: Macrocytosis (high MCV) is commonly caused by Vitamin B12 or Folate deficiency, thyroid disease, or liver conditions.
lifestyle_guidance: Consume adequate green leafy vegetables, legumes, and vitamin-fortified foods.
clinical_follow_up: Iron studies (Ferritin) and Vitamin B12 / Folate levels.
source: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

description: Neutrophils are the most abundant white blood cells, acting as rapid responders to acute bacterial infections and tissue damage.
low_implication: Neutropenia leaves the body vulnerable to bacterial and fungal infections.
high_implication: Neutrophilia typically indicates active bacterial infection, acute injury, or inflammatory flare-ups.
lifestyle_guidance: Ensure thorough handwashing and food hygiene.
clinical_follow_up: Absolute Neutrophil Count (ANC) and clinical infection screen.

description: Creatinine is a waste product generated from muscle metabolism and filtered out of the blood entirely by healthy kidneys.
low_implication: Low creatinine is generally harmless and can reflect low muscle mass, rigorous vegetarian diet, or advanced age.
high_implication: Elevated creatinine indicates decreased kidney clearance, potentially due to dehydration, kidney infection, medication toxicity, or chronic kidney disease (CKD).
lifestyle_guidance: Maintain proper daily hydration, minimize excessive intake of high-dose NSAID pain relievers, and control blood pressure.
clinical_follow_up: eGFR calculation, Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN), urine routine for protein/albumin, and ultrasound of kidneys if persistent.

description: Urea is formed in the liver as an end product of protein breakdown and is excreted by the kidneys.
low_implication: Low urea may be seen in low-protein diets, severe malnutrition, or overhydration.
high_implication: Elevated urea reflects impaired renal excretion, dehydration, high protein catabolism, or gastrointestinal bleeding.
lifestyle_guidance: Drink adequate water throughout the day and balance dietary protein intake.
clinical_follow_up: Correlate with Serum Creatinine and hydration status.

description: Uric acid is produced when the body breaks down purines found in certain foods and body tissues.
low_implication: Low levels are uncommon and usually of little clinical concern.
high_implication: Hyperuricemia can crystallize in joints causing painful gout attacks or form kidney stones.
lifestyle_guidance: Limit purine-rich foods (red meat, organ meats, shellfish, beer, high-fructose corn syrup). Drink plenty of water.
clinical_follow_up: Joint evaluation if experiencing toe/foot pain; renal ultrasound if history of stones.
source: American College of Rheumatology & Mayo Clinic

description: Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT/SGPT) is an enzyme primarily concentrated inside liver cells.
low_implication: Low ALT levels are normal and expected in healthy individuals.
high_implication: Elevated ALT suggests hepatocellular stress or inflammation, seen in fatty liver disease (NAFLD/NASH), viral hepatitis, alcohol use, or medication effects.
lifestyle_guidance: Maintain a healthy weight, limit saturated fats and refined sugars, avoid alcohol, and exercise regularly.
clinical_follow_up: Complete Liver Function Test, Viral Hepatitis panel (HBsAg, Anti-HCV), and abdominal ultrasound.
source: American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD)

description: Aspartate Aminotransferase (AST/SGOT) is an enzyme found in the liver, heart, skeletal muscles, and kidneys.
low_implication: Low AST levels are typical and healthy.
high_implication: Elevated AST reflects tissue injury in liver, muscle, or heart; compare with ALT to assess hepatic origin.
lifestyle_guidance: Reduce intake of ultra-processed foods, moderate alcohol, and engage in steady cardiovascular exercise.
clinical_follow_up: AST/ALT ratio assessment, LFT recheck, and CPK if muscle soreness is present.

description: Bilirubin is a yellowish compound formed during the natural breakdown of aged red blood cells.
low_implication: Low bilirubin is generally benign.
high_implication: Elevated bilirubin causes jaundice (yellowing of skin/eyes), dark urine, and can indicate biliary obstruction, hepatitis, or rapid hemolysis.
lifestyle_guidance: Stay hydrated, eat light easily digestible meals, and avoid liver-toxic substances.
clinical_follow_up: Fractionate into Direct and Indirect Bilirubin; abdominal ultrasound for bile duct assessment.

description: Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP) is an enzyme concentrated in the bile ducts of the liver and in bone tissue.
low_implication: Rarely indicates zinc deficiency or hypophosphatasia.
high_implication: High ALP can stem from biliary obstruction/cholestasis, bone growth/healing, or bone disorders (e.g. Paget's disease).
lifestyle_guidance: Adequate dietary calcium and vitamin D for bone health.
clinical_follow_up: GGT test to distinguish liver vs. bone origin; abdominal imaging if biliary suspicion.

description: Total cholesterol measures the cumulative amount of cholesterol (HDL, LDL, VLDL) in your blood.
low_implication: Very low cholesterol may be linked to severe malnutrition, hyperthyroidism, or malabsorption.
high_implication: Elevated total cholesterol contributes to atherosclerotic plaque buildup, increasing long-term cardiovascular risk.
lifestyle_guidance: Adopt a heart-healthy Mediterranean diet rich in soluble fiber, omega-3 fatty acids, nuts, and whole grains. Avoid trans fats.
clinical_follow_up: Full lipid fraction assessment and 10-year cardiovascular risk score evaluation.

description: High-Density Lipoprotein ('good cholesterol') transports excess cholesterol from tissues back to the liver for clearance.
low_implication: Low HDL increases vulnerability to coronary artery disease, especially in combination with high triglycerides.
high_implication: High HDL is generally protective against cardiovascular disease.
lifestyle_guidance: Regular aerobic exercise, smoking cessation, and consuming healthy monounsaturated fats (olive oil, avocados) help boost HDL.
clinical_follow_up: Assess Total Cholesterol/HDL ratio.
source: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)

description: Low-Density Lipoprotein ('bad cholesterol') deposits cholesterol onto arterial walls, promoting plaque formation.
low_implication: Optimal for cardiovascular health, especially in individuals with diabetes or preexisting heart disease.
high_implication: Elevated LDL significantly accelerates arterial narrowing and increases risk of myocardial infarction or stroke.
lifestyle_guidance: Reduce dietary saturated fats, avoid trans fats, consume oats, beans, psyllium husk, and maintain regular physical activity.
clinical_follow_up: Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk estimation; discuss statin therapy with physician if indicated.

description: Triglycerides are the most common type of fat in the blood, stored for future energy between meals.
low_implication: Low levels are generally benign.
high_implication: High triglycerides correlate with metabolic syndrome, insulin resistance, and fatty liver; extreme levels (>500 mg/dL) risk acute pancreatitis.
lifestyle_guidance: Significantly cut down on refined sugars, sweet beverages, alcohol, and refined carbohydrates. Increase physical activity.
clinical_follow_up: Evaluate fasting blood glucose, HbA1c, and thyroid function.

description: Thyroid Stimulating Hormone, released by the pituitary gland, regulates the production of thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3).
low_implication: Suppressed TSH (<0.4 uIU/mL) suggests hyperthyroidism (overactive thyroid), causing tremors, palpitations, heat intolerance, and unintended weight loss.
high_implication: Elevated TSH (>4.0 uIU/mL) signals primary hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid), leading to fatigue, weight gain, constipation, dry skin, and cold sensitivity.
lifestyle_guidance: Ensure adequate dietary iodine and selenium intake. Take thyroid medications strictly on an empty stomach if prescribed.
clinical_follow_up: Free T3, Free T4, and Anti-TPO antibody testing.

description: Blood glucose is the primary sugar circulating in the bloodstream, providing energy to cells.
low_implication: Hypoglycemia (<70 mg/dL) can cause shaking, sweating, dizziness, confusion, and requires immediate carbohydrate consumption.
high_implication: Hyperglycemia indicates impaired glucose tolerance, insulin resistance, or diabetes mellitus.
lifestyle_guidance: Follow a low glycemic index diet, eat consistent meals, avoid sugary drinks, and engage in daily 30-minute walks.
clinical_follow_up: Confirm with HbA1c and oral glucose tolerance test if screening fasting sugar is elevated.
source: American Diabetes Association (ADA) Standards of Care

description: Glycated hemoglobin reflects your average blood glucose levels over the preceding 2 to 3 months.
low_implication: Values <4.0% are rare and may relate to hemolytic anemia or frequent hypoglycemia.
high_implication: 5.7% to 6.4% indicates prediabetes; 6.5% or higher on two separate tests confirms diabetes mellitus.
lifestyle_guidance: Structured lifestyle modification: weight loss of 5-7%, regular aerobic and resistance exercise, portion control.
clinical_follow_up: Fasting blood sugar profile, microalbuminuria urine test, and annual retinal eye exam.

description: 25-Hydroxy Vitamin D is crucial for calcium absorption, bone mineralization, and immune regulation.
low_implication: Deficiency (<20 ng/mL) causes bone pain, muscle weakness, osteopenia/osteoporosis, and increased risk of fractures.
high_implication: Hypervitaminosis D is rare and typically occurs only with massive supplement overdoses, causing hypercalcemia.
lifestyle_guidance: Safe sunlight exposure (15-20 minutes mid-morning), fortified dairy or plant milk, egg yolks, and fatty fish.
clinical_follow_up: Consult physician regarding weekly therapeutic Vitamin D3 supplementation (e.g. 60,000 IU) followed by maintenance.
source: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements & Endocrine Society

description: Cobalamin is vital for nerve function, neurological health, and DNA and red blood cell synthesis.
low_implication: Deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia, numbness/tingling in hands and feet (peripheral neuropathy), memory lapses, and fatigue.
high_implication: High B12 is often incidental due to recent multivitamin intake, but can rarely reflect liver or myeloproliferative conditions.
lifestyle_guidance: Strict vegetarians/vegans should regularly consume B12-fortified foods or oral supplements.
clinical_follow_up: Check Serum Homocysteine or Methylmalonic Acid (MMA) if borderline; oral or intramuscular supplementation.

description: Sodium is the primary extracellular electrolyte maintaining fluid balance, blood pressure, and neuromuscular signaling.
low_implication: Hyponatremia causes nausea, headache, lethargy, muscle cramps, and in acute cases confusion or seizures.
high_implication: Hypernatremia usually reflects dehydration, excessive fluid loss, or high salt intake.
lifestyle_guidance: Balance fluid and sodium intake based on clinical advice; avoid rapid unguided electrolyte changes.
clinical_follow_up: Urine sodium and osmolality; evaluate diuretic or medication usage.

description: Potassium is essential for normal cardiac electrical rhythm, skeletal muscle contraction, and fluid balance.
low_implication: Hypokalemia (<3.5 mEq/L) can cause cardiac arrhythmias, muscle weakness, and fatigue.
high_implication: Hyperkalemia (>5.0 mEq/L, especially >6.0 mEq/L) is a medical emergency that can trigger lethal heart arrhythmias.
lifestyle_guidance: Do not take unprescribed potassium supplements without physician monitoring.
clinical_follow_up: Urgent ECG if significantly abnormal; rule out hemolyzed sample artifact.

description: C-Reactive Protein is an acute-phase protein synthesized by the liver in response to systemic inflammation or infection.
low_implication: Low levels indicate minimal systemic inflammation, which is normal and desirable.
high_implication: Significantly elevated CRP points to active bacterial infections, autoimmune inflammatory disorders (e.g. RA, lupus), or tissue trauma.
lifestyle_guidance: Anti-inflammatory dietary patterns (rich in berries, olive oil, leafy greens) and regular physical activity.
clinical_follow_up: Clinical evaluation for underlying infection, ESR, and autoimmune markers.
